title: Passing Away of the Three
body:
Passing Away of the Three

Fifteen years passed in peace. Yudhishthira ruled Hastinapur with absolute justice, treating the blind Dhritarashtra and Queen Gandhari with the highest respect and tenderness. Yet, Dhritarashtra's heart remained secretly anchored to his grief. One day, the old king summoned Yudhishthira to his chambers: 'My child, I have spent fifteen happy years under your roof. My sons perished due to their own sins. The time has now come for Gandhari and me to retire to the forest, to wear bark and tattered rags, and spend our final days in prayer and severe penance, as did our ancestors. Pray, grant us your permission.'
Yudhishthira was deeply shocked and fell at his feet, pleading that he would gladly give up the crown and follow them to the forest to serve them. But Sage Vyasa entered the chamber and counseled Yudhishthira: 'Do what Dhritarashtra, the eldest of the Kurus, desires. Let him depart. The dharma of kings is to die in battle or to spend their last days in the forest. Do not stand in their way.'
With a heavy heart, Yudhishthira consented. The next morning, the blind king stepped out of Hastinapur, his hand resting on Gandhari's shoulder. Gandhari, who had bound her own eyes out of devotion to her blind husband, placed her hand on Kuntidevi's shoulder for guidance.
As they walked out of the city gates, Yudhishthira realized with horror that Kunti also intended to stay in the forest forever. He wept and pleaded with his mother: 'Mother, not thus! You blessed us and sent us to battle. It is not right you should now desert us to live in the forest!' Kunti remained firm, turning her tearful eyes upon her eldest son: 'Remember with love Karna who died a hero's death. Look after Draupadi with tenderness. Do not give cause for grief to Bhima, Arjuna, Nakula, and Sahadeva. I must join my husband Pandu. May your mind ever stand steady on dharma.' The three elderly monarchs walked slowly into the forest depths. Within three years, they voluntarily gave up their bodies in a sudden forest fire, sitting in deep yogic postures, letting their souls merge with the Paramatma.
